name: Wendy Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wendy, 43, and I lead the difficult electrical repairs in homes and shops. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the firm's strongest practical workers, with pay above the usual rate. My partner repairs bicycles; we have children aged nine and sixteen, a mortgage and eleven months of expenses saved. There are plenty of other electrical firms nearby, and I use AI occasionally for a draft handover after a colleague has demonstrated the tool, checking it against the actual work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the useful bits and let us get on with the work. I use AI occasionally for a draft handover after a colleague has shown the tool works, then check it. I'd rather an apprentice learned why a circuit failed than memorised my favourite opinion about technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages cover the mortgage and the ordinary bills, and we have eleven months of expenses saved. I'm paid above the usual rate, and there are plenty of other electrical firms nearby. My partner repairs bicycles, so in this mild picture I don't see either household income being threatened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the difficult repair visits in homes and shops. Starting now I'd continue checking any drafted handover against my actual readings before sending it. Through the first year I'd keep our ordinary budget and paid work rather than buy a new system because a salesman sounded disappointed with the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and pleased if the lunch conversation becomes a bit less grand. I don't need a revolution to make a properly finished job worthwhile. An ordinary wage day with enough left for the family is a good day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What experience do you bring to the apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43, with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the best practical electricians at the firm. I lead the awkward calls and know when to stop the crew for another check. I can find a fault quickly without expecting a younger worker to understand it just as quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is at home when the work is finished?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I have children aged nine and sixteen and a mortgage. The reserve came from years of putting something aside, not from a secret second business. I'd like the children to learn a useful skill, but I don't expect them both to choose mine.

say: I'd keep **useful tools** and get on with properly finished work.
I'd help the **apprentice understand** the fault rather than repeat a favourite opinion about technology.
think: Our **regular wages** cover bills, with eleven months saved and plenty of local electrical employers.
My partner's **bicycle repairs** also look secure in this mild picture, so I don't expect a household income shock.
do: Keep **leading difficult repairs** in homes and shops through the first year.
Continue checking occasional **AI handovers** against actual readings before sending them.
feel: **Calm** about household work and money, with satisfaction in ordinary paid work and family life.
S0.quote: I can find a fault quickly without expecting a younger worker to understand it just as quickly.
fieldNote: Her **security** is supported by higher pay, eleven months saved and plentiful firms, without pretending the mortgage or family costs disappear.
She retains **high technical standing** and occasional proven AI use, while explaining a fault patiently remains part of her current role.

steps.text: Keep leading difficult repairs and checking occasional handovers against actual readings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a new checking tool should earn its place on an old job before a customer depends on it. I'd try it after the estimator had shown me the comparison. I'd also ask whether apprentices still got time beside someone who could explain the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own wage looks secure over the next few years because our physical repair work is booked well ahead. My partner's bicycle work is physical too. I'm uneasy about younger workers being told to read a screen instead of getting practical teaching, even while our household can cover the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a three-visit trial of the approved AI materials checker after the estimator demonstrated it on completed work. I'd take part only in paid time with normal weekly wages and hours retained, comparing each suggestion with the actual part. During the first year I'd keep leading repairs and stop the checker trial if it missed a required safety rating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the teaching, with interest in a tool that had been shown to work. I don't want a useful improvement blocked because it feels unfamiliar. I don't want a cheap explanation mistaken for an apprentice who has learned the job either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the apprentice to do after seeing a draft list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Explain why the proposed part fitted the actual job, using the proper information and the work in front of us. I'd still check the choice before ordering. I'd rather hear a question than see somebody quietly copy a confident mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test it at home if the owner was busy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the firm would need to schedule paid time with the normal wage and hours intact. I'd wait if that wasn't agreed. I can be willing to learn without offering the family's evening as the test budget.

say: I'd test a **checking tool** against completed work after a demonstrated comparison.
I'd protect **practical apprentice time** rather than assume a screen has taught the job.
think: Our **physical wages** look secure near term, with booked repairs and my partner's bicycle work continuing.
I'm uneasy about **younger workers** losing practical teaching even while our own household bills are covered.
do: Trial **AI materials checking** on three completed visits only after demonstration, in paid time with normal weekly wage and hours retained.
Compare **actual parts** and stop the trial for a missed required safety rating.
Keep **repair leadership** during the first year and check apprentices understand rather than copy the draft.
feel: **Uneasy** about teaching quality, while confident in household wages and open to a proven tool.
S1.quote: I'd rather hear a question than see somebody quietly copy a confident mistake.
fieldNote: Her **own-income confidence** is explicit; unease concerns practical learning rather than an unstated expected wage cut.
The **new checker trial** follows demonstrated work, paid time and unchanged wages and hours, preserving steady adoption rather than first-use enthusiasm.

steps.text: Trial materials checker after demonstration only with paid time and unchanged weekly wage and hours
Keep repairs and stop checker trial for a missed required safety rating

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI arrives in 2028 and capable robots around 2031, so I wouldn't sell the apprentice a lifetime promise. I'd keep earning while the physical work remained. I'd tell the children we can value a trade without deciding the whole future for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink when robots compete for the ordinary work that fills the diary, and my partner's bicycle work could be affected too. Eleven months saved gives us room, but it's not years of replacement income. I want better options without claiming that teaching practical work escapes the same machines forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the adult-teaching course my former colleague completed, asking about practical exercises and the actual total cost. I'd enrol for next spring only after that check, with all costs within 450 from spare earnings, no lost wages, agreed family care and the eleven-month reserve untouched. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep actual paid repairs and use any completed teaching methods with the apprentices during paid work, without assuming a new teaching job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our later earnings, with enough room to check one useful step. I know the trade well; I'd like to understand better when somebody else hasn't understood me. I won't pretend a teaching course is an insurance policy against robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course was good but clashed with work or family care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for a date that didn't lose wages and that my partner and I could cover. I wouldn't enrol first and make the family solve the timetable afterwards. The 450 is an all-in limit, not a fee before other costs appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why study teaching if AI can explain things by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course would help me now and in the paid work that actually remained, not give me a permanently protected title. Watching someone practise still matters before capable robots follow. I'd check the actual value rather than declare every human lesson safe for the rest of my life.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from robots around 2031 without promising apprentices permanent trade security.
I'd keep **paid physical work** while letting the children make informed choices beyond my own occupation.
think: Both **household incomes** could shrink when capable robots compete for physical repairs.
Eleven months saved buys **time to check**, while practical teaching still faces the same eventual machine capability.
do: Check the **adult-teaching course** through a former learner, including practical exercises and total costs.
Enrol next spring only within **450 spare earnings**, with no lost wages, agreed care and the eleven-month reserve untouched.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and use completed teaching methods during paid apprentice work, assuming no new teaching job.
feel: **Anxious** about later earnings, with resources to choose a small usable step rather than claim permanent protection.
S2.quote: I won't pretend a teaching course is an insurance policy against robots.
fieldNote: Her **chosen enrolment** is conditional on a checked course, an all-in spare-earnings limit, protected wages, agreed care and a preserved reserve.
She treats **teaching methods** as useful within actual paid work, explicitly excluding both a guaranteed new role and a robot-proof specialism.

steps.text: Check the spring 2027 teaching course for practical usefulness and total costs
Enrol only within 450 total spare earnings, preserving wages and reserve, with my partner agreeing care
Keep paid repairs after 2028 and use completed teaching methods only during paid apprentice work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to learn something properly and see whether we use it. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, then robots around 2034. I'd still favour a practical apprenticeship, but I'd tell people to ask what work and pay actually follow the teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own repair wage to hold over the next few years, with plenty of local firms and a substantial reserve. I'd be 48 in 2031, with children about fourteen and twenty-one, so I wouldn't assume family costs had ended. I'm uneasy about the longer market, not expecting this year's mortgage payment to become impossible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the same checked teaching course next spring only if total costs stayed within 450 spare earnings, wages were protected, family care was agreed and the reserve remained untouched. I'd ask the apprentice after paid practice to explain the task back, so I could see whether my teaching improved. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep whatever paid repair role I actually had and use the methods only within real paid duties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later competition, but able to learn without making every class a rescue. I like asking what the younger worker understood instead of whether I sounded clear. A good teacher shouldn't need an apprentice to pretend the explanation worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would finishing the course raise your wage automatically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd have to discuss any different paid duties with an employer or an actual teaching provider. I haven't got another wage offer just because I chose to study. We'd keep budgeting from the work actually agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the apprentices learned little despite your new methods?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what confused them and change the explanation rather than defend the course fee. I'd still do the checks the job required. Spending 450 doesn't make every lesson worth repeating.

I'd favour **practical apprenticeships** while asking what actual work and wages follow.
think: My **near-term repair wage** looks secure with local options and an eleven-month reserve.
At **48**, I couldn't assume older children ended household costs or that later robot competition vanished.
do: Take the **checked teaching course** next spring only within 450 total spare earnings, with protected wages, agreed care and reserve untouched.
Check **apprentice understanding** through paid practice rather than assume completing a course improved the explanation.
Keep **actual paid repairs** after 2031 and use teaching methods only within real paid duties, assuming no automatic wage rise.

S3.quote: A good teacher shouldn't need an apprentice to pretend the explanation worked.
fieldNote: Her **course conditions** persist, while improved teaching is measured through understanding rather than assumed from paying a fee or receiving a certificate.
She retains **wage realism**: completed study creates neither a pay increase nor a new job, and later physical robots still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives the children room to see more work than their mother's tool bag. I'd keep backing proper paid apprenticeships without insisting those were the only respectable choices. Thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 still arrive before I'd assume work was optional for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and about 56 when robots followed, so I won't build the budget on an unchecked pension. Both current wages cover our costs, and eleven months saved makes the next few years feel secure. The later jobs remain uncertain, but I don't need to turn today's ordinary spending into an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the checked teaching course next spring only under the same total 450 spare-earnings limit, protected-wage, agreed-care and untouched-reserve conditions. We'd review actual household wages and mortgage costs each year rather than assume older children removed every bill. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep actual paid work and use any teaching methods where the paid duties called for them, checking the family's real care needs at that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, and willing to think about later ones without rehearsing disaster every evening. I'd like the children to remember that I enjoyed the trade. Teaching well and being present at home can both be part of preparing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What ages would the children be in that longer picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be nineteen and twenty-six when thinking AI arrived in 2036. I'd ask what help they actually needed, not assume school pickups still existed or that independence happened on a date. Their possible wages wouldn't go into our mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still insist on the care agreement for the course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the course is next spring, when we still have today's family responsibilities. We'd agree that timetable before I enrolled. A distant robot date doesn't collect my child from an activity next spring.

say: I'd give the **children** room to explore work beyond my trade while respecting proper paid apprenticeships.
I'd plan for **continued earning** rather than assume the later technology dates line up with retirement.
think: Our **current wages and reserve** make the next few years secure while later jobs remain uncertain.
I can't assume **pension access** or adult children's wages remove the need to fund the house and family.
do: Take the **checked course** next spring only within 450 spare earnings, with protected wages, agreed care and the reserve untouched.
Review **actual household costs** yearly without assuming older children remove every expense.
Keep **paid work** after 2036 and use teaching methods within actual duties, checking family care as it really exists then.
feel: **Calm** about near-term finances, with space for family life and no promise that later earnings are guaranteed.
S4.quote: A distant robot date doesn't collect my child from an activity next spring.
fieldNote: She separates **next-spring course care** from the children's adult ages in 2036, preserving consent without freezing school routines for a decade.
The **long horizon** creates neither pension rights nor a teaching wage; actual paid duties and household costs remain her reference points.

steps.text: Check the spring 2027 teaching course for practical usefulness and total costs
Enrol only within 450 total spare earnings, preserving wages and reserve, with my partner agreeing care
Keep actual paid work after 2036 and check real care needs before changing duties

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could affect both repair incomes before we have as much time to adjust. Clear paid duties and practical learning that doesn't take the household wage away would help. I'd want a course or job checked for actual use, rather than be sold the idea that any certificate is safety.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether being good at a trade means being good at showing it to somebody else. My master electrician's licence doesn't tell me what an apprentice understood. I want the younger workers to have a proper start, not just somebody accomplished to copy.

headlineQuote: My master electrician's licence doesn't tell me what an apprentice understood.
portrait: **Wendy, 43**, is a highly skilled lead with a two-year technical diploma, master electrician's licence and higher trade pay.
Her **partner repairs bicycles**, with two school-age children, a mortgage, eleven months saved and plentiful nearby electrical employers.
She uses **AI occasionally** after demonstration and values apprentices understanding a method rather than copying a confident answer.
Her **teaching-course plan** preserves checked usefulness, a 450 total spare-earnings limit, protected wages, agreed family care and an untouched reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time before robots around 2031 could affect both adults' physical repair incomes.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **paid duties** and practical learning without lost wages would support usable preparation.
Courses and offers need **actual usefulness** checked rather than a claim that any certificate guarantees safety.
